B: Between stimulus and response there is a space. In that space is our power to choose our response.
D: Viktor Frankl, Man's Search for Meaning
E:
Maybe the most important sentence ever written about emotional intelligence — and it has nothing to do with age. All of us live in that gap between something happening and how we answer it.

The skill is widening the gap. Naming what you feel before you react measurably calms the brain's alarm center, the amygdala — "name it to tame it" (Lieberman et al., 2007). The pause is where the grown-up lives.

B: Knowing yourself is the beginning of all wisdom.
E:
Two thousand years on, it's still step one. You can't manage a feeling you can't name or an urge you don't notice.

Self-awareness is the ground floor of emotional intelligence — every other skill is built on it (Goleman's model). It's also the part that never finishes; we're all still getting acquainted with ourselves.

👉 What have you only recently understood about yourself?

B: The curious paradox is that when I accept myself just as I am, then I can change.
D: Carl Rogers, On Becoming a Person, 1961
E:
The paradox that frees people: change doesn't start with fixing yourself, it starts with accepting yourself.

The research agrees. Self-compassion — treating yourself like someone you're rooting for — predicts more resilience and motivation than self-criticism, which mostly keeps us stuck (Kristin Neff).

B: The childhood shows the man, as morning shows the day.
E:
The through-line of this whole feed: the kid you were is still shaping the adult you are. Everyone carries a childhood, whether or not they're raising one.

That's not only poetry — early emotional experiences wire lasting patterns in how we handle stress and connection (ACE research, Felitti & Anda, 1998). The hopeful part: wiring can be rewired.

👉 What would your younger self be glad you finally learned?

B: In a very real sense we have two minds, one that thinks and one that feels.
E:
From the researcher who put "emotional intelligence" on the map. The thinking brain and the feeling brain are different systems — and when feelings run hot, they can hijack the thinking one.

The fix isn't to switch feelings off; it's to get the two talking. That integration is exactly what EQ trains, at any age.

👉 When did your feeling-brain outvote your thinking-brain?

B: Emotional intelligence is the single biggest predictor of performance in the workplace.
E:
A fact for the skeptics: across 500,000+ people, EQ explained more about job performance than IQ or personality, and 90% of top performers scored high on it (TalentSmart).

Translation — the thing we practice for kids is the same thing quietly running adult life, meetings included.

👉 Where would more emotional intelligence help you most right now?

B: Inside every older person is a younger person wondering what happened.
E:
Funny because it's a little devastating. We don't outgrow the kid we were — we just get taller and busier.

Which is the point: tending your own emotions isn't childish, it's the same homework at every age. That wondering-what-happened kid is still worth checking in on.

👉 What would your younger self be surprised to see about your life now?

B: We never really grow up, we only learn how to act in public.
E:
The group chat versus the boardroom. "Maturity" is often just a better poker face, not fewer feelings.

And that's fine — emotional intelligence was never about having no big feelings, it's knowing they're there and choosing what to do with them (self-regulation).

👉 What feeling are you best at hiding in public?

B: Every man is a damn fool for at least five minutes every day; wisdom consists in not exceeding the limit.
E:
A permission slip for being human. Nobody regulates perfectly — the goal was never a flawless day, just a shorter recovery.

Resilience research backs it: it's not about avoiding the five bad minutes, it's how quickly you find your way back (emotional repair).

B: Owning our story and loving ourselves through that process is the bravest thing we'll ever do.
D: Brené Brown, The Gifts of Imperfection, 2010
E:
From a researcher who spent decades studying shame and courage. Facing your own story — messy parts included — is the brave thing nobody hands you a medal for.

Her data is clear: people who can be vulnerable and self-compassionate turn out more resilient and more connected, not less.

👉 What part of your story are you learning to own?

B: Feelings are much like waves: we can't stop them from coming, but we can choose which to surf.
E:
The whole philosophy of emotional intelligence in one image. You don't get to cancel the ocean — you learn to swim in it.

That's the shift from being flooded to being able to notice a feeling, name it, and ride it out. It's a skill, and skills are learnable at any age.

B: You don't have to attend every argument you're invited to.
E:
The pettiest superpower, and one everyone needs. Not every provocation deserves a reply; sometimes silence is the most emotionally intelligent answer in the room.

Choosing not to react is the adult version of the pause — the same brake we hope kids build, still being practiced by all of us.
